1.content: Create a native desktop app with Rust and open your first window.

2.content: macOS 14 or later Rust 1.90 or later Bun 1.4 or later Xcode Command Line Tools ( xcode-select --install ) macOS is the supported target today.

3.content: init writes the project and installs dependencies. Omit --language to choose Go, TypeScript, or Rust interactively.

4.content: The generated src/main.rs opens a window. Keep state on your View and call cx.invalidate() after you change it. on_reopen opens a window again when the user clicks the Dock icon and none are visible.

5.content: dev rebuilds as you edit. build writes a packaged app under dist/ .

6.content: Write components . Keep them in sync with view state . Add styles and layout .

7.content: The files in a QuickGUI Rust project and how to configure them. A Rust project keeps application code in a Cargo package and development commands in a small Bun package.

8.content: Commit Cargo.lock after the first successful build. Split larger apps into ordinary Rust modules.

9.content: src/main.rs starts Application::new().run(...) and opens windows from that callback. Each window owns a View . entry in the config is the crate directory.

10.content: The application icon comes from resources/icon.png . Extra files can be listed in resources . See App Icon and Bundled Resources . TOML supports the same keys. The CLI reads quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . Enable optional crate features in Cargo.toml instead of setting extensions in the app config.

11.content: Applications depend on the quickgui crate. @quickgui/cli is a development dependency. Optional terminal , markdown , editor , and updater capabilities are Cargo features. Keep the crate version already in your project:

13.content: Write views, compose children, and use the built-in control set. Implement View for screens that keep state. Functions that return Element work for stateless pieces.

14.content: Child views can also be functions that return Element when they have no state of their own.

15.content: div , text , button , text_input , text_area , img , svg , custom_shader , and VirtualList are the building blocks. submit_button submits the nearest form . Markdown uses features = ["markdown"] ; Editor , CodeBlock , and DiffView use features = ["editor"] ; Terminal is also optional.

16.content: Keep parts under the root they belong to so focus and values stay connected.

17.content: Store values on the view, pass them into constructors, and update them from listeners. Then call cx.invalidate() . The view owns the state.

18.content: The component reference covers forms, overlays, menus, tables, trees, and more. examples/base_ui_components.rs is a gallery.

19.content: Apply fluent style methods on each visible part. Parts ship unstyled so colors and layout belong to your app. Types such as TabsState and SelectState expose the current state for custom presentation.

20.content: Store view state and redraw when it changes. Store state on the View . render reads that state to build elements. Call cx.invalidate() after a mutation so the window redraws.

21.content: Keep fields on the view struct. Register listeners with cx.listener so events can mutate those fields. A value you copy in render is the current frame’s snapshot.

22.content: Compute derived values in render from the fields you already store. Store an expensive derivation on the view when several children need the same value in one frame.

23.content: Start external work from listeners or Application callbacks, and stop it when the view is dropped. Closing a window drops the view and its listeners.

24.content: Calling cx.invalidate() marks the window dirty. Multiple invalidations in one event become one render. Do not install a timer to redraw when nothing changed.

25.content: Show and hide content, render lists, and work with the current window. View::render builds the UI after you invalidate or the operating system asks for a redraw. Use id so rows keep their identity across renders.

26.content: Return impl IntoElement from render . The window sleeps until invalidate or a platform event.

27.content: Omitting a branch drops those nodes.

28.content: Give stateful rows stable id s. For long collections, use VirtualList or Table .

29.content: Each open_window owns an independent view. Closing one window does not drop the others. Handle the Dock icon by opening a new window when has_visible_windows is false.

31.content: examples/base_ui_components.rs is the UI gallery. Enable the inspector crate feature for the in-app inspector.

32.content: Lay out and style views with Flexbox, Grid, and interaction states. Fluent methods set layout, paint, typography, and interaction styles. Lengths are logical pixels.

33.content: Presets such as flex_col , p_3 , rounded_lg , and text_lg match the Go and TypeScript helpers. p_3 is 12 pixels. For custom values, use rounded(10.0) , p(14.0) , and w / h .

37.content: Use grid plus track, placement, and span methods.

38.content: Font family, weight, size, wrapping, and selection apply to text. Colors accept Color::rgb8 , Color::rgba8 , and packed values.

40.content: Name a group on an ancestor and use group_hover on descendants so they style together.

41.content: Build text fields, checkboxes, radios, and select controls. Pass the current value into text_input / text_area and write edits from on_input .

45.content: SelectState , ComboboxState , and AutocompleteState hold the current value and options. Keep option values stable.

46.content: Input listeners receive the next text. Register pointer, key, and submit handlers on ViewContext .

47.content: Show popovers, dialogs, and operating-system file pickers. Use a QuickGUI overlay for app-styled content, or a system dialog for file picking and alerts.

48.content: Compose trigger, positioner, popup, and arrow parts. Store open on the view.

49.content: Dialog::new and Dialog::alert add a title, description, backdrop, and close control.

50.content: SystemPopover opens a native child window, which can extend past the owner window’s edge.

52.content: Declare routes, nested layouts, and in-app navigation. Declare routes, render the match in the current window, and navigate with push / replace .

53.content: RouteDefinition::layout declares a pathless ancestor. Relative child paths join their parent; an absolute child path starts at the root.

54.content: Match the route chain and wrap inner content with layout elements. Pathless layouts appear in the match without adding a URL segment.

55.content: The controller supports push , replace , back , and forward . Navigation stays inside the app.

57.content: Animate hover, color, and opacity, and play GIF or WebP images. Animate style changes with transition . The view does not rebuild for each frame.

59.content: Change a style field from view state and call invalidate . Keep the element mounted while it animates.

60.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Timing and frame rate
60.content: Transition::new takes a Duration . Set easing with with_easing and optionally cap cadence with max_fps .

61.content: Background, border color and width, radius, text color, box shadow, opacity, and transform interpolate. Width, height, and padding do not.

62.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Mounting and reduced motion
62.content: Keep an overlay mounted during its exit transition when the component supports that. Transitions follow the system Reduce Motion setting.

63.content: img plays GIF and WebP files from the path you pass. You do not need a timer.

64.content: Open windows and use menus, clipboard, dialogs, and file watching. Call Application::new().run(...) once from main . Its startup callback creates windows.

65.content: cx.open_window(WindowOptions::new("Title").size(width, height), view) creates a window with its own View . Closing the window drops that view. Handle the Dock icon with Application::on_reopen when has_visible_windows is false.

66.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Commands and services
66.content: Typed APIs cover dialogs, clipboard, shell, appearance, menus, and displays. Capture cx.window_handle() during a listener when later work needs that window. Tray icons are covered in Tray Icon .

67.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Events and file watching
67.content: Window events include focus, resize, appearance, minimize, fullscreen, and close. Application callbacks include reopen, activation, quit, and open URLs. Enable the file-watcher crate feature when you need filesystem events, and drop watchers with the owning view.

70.content: Buttons, toggles, sliders, steppers, progress views, gauges, text and secure fields, pickers, segmented controls, date and color pickers, and popovers.

74.content: Style SwiftUI controls and nest QuickGUI content inside them. Apply SwiftUiModifier values in declaration order. Convenience builders such as style , control_size , and disabled append those modifiers.

80.content: Use resources/icon.png as the packaged application icon, or change the window or Dock icon at runtime. The packaged application icon is the image Finder, the Dock, the Windows taskbar, Start Menu, and Linux desktop launchers show for your app. Put a PNG at resources/icon.png . You can also change a window icon or the macOS Dock icon while the app is running.

81.content: Add a square PNG that is at least 256×256 pixels at resources/icon.png . 1024×1024 is a good source. quickgui build resizes it to every size macOS, Windows, and Linux need. The CLI writes .icns for macOS, .ico for the Windows installer, and the Freedesktop hicolor sizes for Linux. Development reloads skip generated containers; production builds and a configured macos.icon still install an icon. Optional resources/icon.iconset/icon_<n>x<n>.png files replace a generated size with a hand-drawn one. That folder is a build input and is not copied into the packaged app. Set icon in the CLI config only when the source PNG lives somewhere other than resources/icon.png .

82.content: Use these when you already have a platform container: resources/icon.icns is used on macOS when macos.icon is omitted. resources/icon.ico is used by the NSIS installer when windows.icon is omitted. linux.icon is a square PNG used when both resources/icon.png and icon are omitted. macos.icon must be an .icns . windows.icon is an .ico . These config paths override the files in resources/ . Document-type icons are a basename inside the packaged resources. See Bundled Resources .

83.hierarchy: App Icon › Window and Dock icons
83.content: The packaged icon is the application identity. A window can show a different image on Windows and X11: After the window exists, cx.set_window_icon(icon) and cx.clear_window_icon() update that image. On macOS, windows do not have their own icon. Use cx.set_dock_icon(icon) to replace the Dock image for this process. Menu-bar and notification-area icons are a different image. See Tray Icon .

84.content: Target Sizes macOS .icns 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 Windows .ico 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256 Linux hicolor 16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256, 512 Every listed size is generated from the source PNG. The source must be square, at least 256×256, and at most 16 MiB.

85.content: Add a menu-bar or notification-area icon, and mark macOS template images by filename or flag. A tray icon lives in the macOS menu bar, the Windows notification area, or a Linux StatusNotifierItem host. Put the artwork in resources/ and create the icon from the application startup callback. This is separate from the packaged App Icon .

86.hierarchy: Tray Icon › Create a tray icon
86.content: Ship a small PNG with the app, then create the icon from its packaged path: set_tray_icon replaces the icon with that id. remove_tray_icon deletes it. Image::open and TrayIconImage::from_path both honor the template filename convention. A 22×22 PNG is a good 1× source. Draw a 44×44 companion as trayTemplate@2x.png when you want a retina menu-bar image.

87.content: On macOS, a template image is a monochrome mask. AppKit recolors it for the menu bar's light, dark, and highlighted appearances using only the alpha channel. A filename whose stem ends in Template , optionally followed by @2x or @3x , is treated as a template: trayTemplate.png and statusTemplate@2x.png match. emailTemplateIcon.png does not. quickgui::is_template_image_path is the same check. Call .template(true) or .icon_is_template(true) when the name does not follow that convention, or .template(false) to force the flag off. Image , MenuIcon , and TrayIconImage all carry the flag. Other platforms keep it and ignore it.

88.content: The tray menu is a native context menu. Handle TrayEventKind::MenuItem on Application::on_tray_event . Other kinds are Click , DoubleClick , Enter , Move , Leave , and Scroll . show_tray_menu opens the menu at the cursor on macOS and Windows. Linux hosts own menu presentation and reject that call.

89.content: Platform Host Template images show_tray_menu macOS Menu bar extra Recolored by AppKit Supported Windows Notification area Ignored Supported Linux StatusNotifierItem Ignored Unsupported DesktopIntegrationSupport::current().tray_icons is true on macOS, Windows, and Linux. programmable_tray_popup is macOS and Windows only. Keep at most 32 tray icons.

90.content: Ship files in resources/ and load them from the packaged resource directory. Put application files that are not compiled into the executable in a resources/ directory: images, templates, JSON, and other data. The CLI copies that directory’s contents into the packaged app. The running app reads them from AppPaths::resource_dir() , which does not depend on the launch working directory. To embed bytes at compile time instead, use BundledAssets and Application::assets . Custom fonts are a separate option. See Fonts .

91.content: Each file keeps its path relative to resources/ . resources/hero.png is installed as hero.png . resources/copy/template.txt is installed as copy/template.txt . Destination names must not replace reserved names such as fonts , AppIcon.icns , or quickgui.json . quickgui dev and quickgui build both stage these files. A missing extra path listed in config fails the build. The resources/ directory itself is optional. Rust identity and font paths are written to quickgui.json in the same resource directory.

92.content: Use the resources config option to merge extra files or folders into the same packaged directory. Each extra path is copied under its basename. Do not list the project resources/ folder here; it is included automatically. legal/NOTICE.txt is installed as NOTICE.txt . vendor/data is installed as data/ .

93.content: Platform Resource directory macOS .app Contents/Resources Linux AppDir, AppImage, and .deb Next to the executable ( usr/bin ) Linux install.sh tarball Next to the executable ( ~/.local/<package>.app/bin ) Windows installer Next to the executable in $INSTDIR Join packaged names onto resource_dir() at runtime; do not read from the project tree or the current working directory.

94.content: img accepts a filesystem path. Other files use the same join: std::fs::read the path, or load a compile-time BundledAssets map when the bytes should live inside the binary. Relative image paths are not resolved against the resource directory.

95.content: fonts lists OpenType files. The CLI copies them into fonts/ inside the resource directory and registers them from quickgui.json before the first window opens. You can also call Application::font with bytes or an asset path. Fonts are not a replacement for resources/ : an image or JSON file still belongs in that directory, in the extra resources list, or in BundledAssets .

96.content: Ship signed automatic updates for macOS, Windows, and Linux. Enable the updater feature on the quickgui crate. The updater is part of the Rust core, so Rust apps call quickgui::updater directly. Go and TypeScript load the same implementation as an extension, with the same feed, key, and install helper.

98.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Configuration › 1. Create a signing key
98.content: Every update is signed with an Ed25519 key. Create the pair once and keep it for the life of the app: installs only accept updates signed by the key they were built with. The command writes quickgui-update.pub and quickgui-update.key . The public key is safe to commit; the config below reads it from update-public-key.pub . The .key file is the secret: store it in a password manager or your CI secret store, never in the repository. If you lose it, existing installs can never update again.

99.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Configuration › 2. Choose where releases are published
99.content: Set updates.target to "github" or "s3" , and fill in the section with the same name. The target decides where --upload sends files and which URLs the app checks, so you never write a feed or download URL yourself. Both sections may stay in the config; only the one target names is used. The feed address is built into the app, so changing target later only affects versions built after the change. Keep publishing to the old target until users have moved over. GitHub Releases needs only the repository. It must be public, because installed apps download updates without credentials. Amazon S3 needs the bucket, its region, and the public HTTPS address that serves it (the bucket's own URL, or a CloudFront domain in front of it). Cloudflare R2, MinIO, and other S3-compatible stores add endpoint , the address of the S3 API. publicUrl is still the address users download from, which for R2 is a custom domain or the bucket's r2.dev URL. The bucket has to allow public reads of the uploaded files; QuickGUI uploads with your credentials but does not change bucket policy. Enable the crate feature. Keep the crate version already in your project:

100.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Configuration › 3. All updates options
100.content: Option Required Meaning publicKey yes Contents of quickgui-update.pub . Embedded in the app and used to verify every update. target yes "github" or "s3" . Chooses which section is used. github.repository with target = "github" owner/name of a public GitHub repository. github.tagPrefix no Release tag is this plus the version. Default "v" , so version 1.2.0 is released as v1.2.0 . s3.bucket with target = "s3" Bucket name. s3.publicUrl with target = "s3" Public HTTPS address that serves the bucket. No query string or credentials. s3.endpoint no S3 API endpoint for non-AWS providers. Omit for AWS. s3.region no Bucket region, or "auto" for R2. s3.prefix no Folder inside the bucket. It is also appended to publicUrl . automaticChecks no Whether new installs check at launch. Default true . A user's own choice is remembered and wins. changelog no Markdown changelog for all versions. The ## x.y.z section matching version becomes the release notes. Default CHANGELOG.md when that file exists. ed25519SecretKey no Path to the private key file for local builds. The QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY environment variable overrides it. manifest no true signs and writes the update feed on every production build, as --update-manifest does.

101.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Configuration › Where the URLs come from
101.content: The target fixes every address. <file> is a name such as appcast-darwin-arm64.xml , and <tag> is tagPrefix plus the version. GitHub S3 Update feed, install.sh , latest-linux-<arch>.txt https://github.com/<repository>/releases/latest/download/<file> <publicUrl>/<prefix>/<file> Installers and update archives https://github.com/<repository>/releases/download/<tag>/<file> <publicUrl>/<prefix>/<file> On GitHub the feed always comes from the release marked Latest . Drafts and pre-releases are never latest, so they do not reach users until you publish them as a normal release. The CLI embeds the version, identifier, feed URL, and public key in the app. Secret keys are never embedded.

102.content: Start one Updater after the application is ready and read its events on the application thread: quickgui::updater_options!() expands to the settings quickgui build embedded. With plain cargo run it is empty, and the updater reports Disabled , as every development build does. Call updater.check().await from a Check for Updates action, updater.install().await from an update banner, and updater.set_automatic_checks(enabled).await from settings. Each resolves when the command is accepted or rejected; results arrive as events. updater.state() returns the latest event without native calls.

103.content: Keep the Updater for the process lifetime; it belongs to the application, not to a window. Dropping it cancels checks and downloads. quit_required means the verified installer is waiting for the app to exit: call cx.exit() after saving work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out and leaves the current app in place. The core tells the helper when the new version has started, and the helper restores the previous version if it never does.

104.content: Platform Update payload Installation macOS ZIP containing the signed .app Sparkle, embedded only with the feature Windows QuickGUI NSIS .exe installer A helper waits for exit, runs the verified installer, then relaunches Linux Type-2 .AppImage , or the install.sh tarball A helper waits for exit and replaces the user-owned AppImage or install directory, restoring it if the new build fails to start Linux .deb packages, system binaries, and root-owned installs report Disabled . Use the platform package manager there. quickgui build also writes <Name>-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz , install.sh , and latest-linux-<arch>.txt . --upload publishes all three, and with GitHub the script has a stable URL: curl -fsSL https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh installs into ~/.local/<package>.app without root, adds the app to the applications menu, and that install keeps itself current. Set linux.tarball = false to skip it.

106.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Publishing › 1. Release from your machine
106.content: Raise version in your config first: apps only install a version higher than their own. Add a ## <version> section to CHANGELOG.md for it. Then give the build the private key and run it with --upload : For GitHub, sign in once with gh auth login (or set GH_TOKEN ). For S3, set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY . --upload builds the app, signs the update files, writes the feed, and publishes everything. It prints each public URL when it finishes. Use --update-manifest instead to sign and write the feed without uploading, for example to inspect dist/ first. Run the command once per target; every target has its own feed, so a Mac never downloads a Linux build.

107.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Publishing › 2. What gets uploaded
107.content: Target Files macOS <Name>.dmg for new users, <Name>-<version>-<target>.zip for updates, appcast-<target>.xml Windows <Name>-<version>-<target>.exe (installer and update), appcast-<target>.xml Linux .AppImage , <Name>-<version>-<target>.tar.gz , .deb if configured, install.sh , latest-linux-<arch>.txt , appcast-<target>.xml Versioned files are uploaded first and the feed last, so the feed never points at a file that is not there yet. On GitHub the first target creates the release <tag> (with this version's changelog section as its description) and later targets add their files to it. Re-running replaces files of the same name.

108.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Publishing › 3. Release from GitHub Actions
108.content: Add the private key as a repository secret named QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), then push a tag that matches the version in your config: The three jobs upload into the same release. The gh CLI is preinstalled on GitHub's runners. macOS builds that you distribute should also pass --sign and --notarize ; Windows needs NSIS ( makensis ) on the runner, and Linux produces an AppImage only when appimagetool is installed (the tarball needs nothing).

109.content: Release notes come from one Markdown changelog that covers every version. When you publish version 1.2.0 , the build takes the section under the ## 1.2.0 heading and ships it with the update. updates.changelog names the file, relative to the project. Leave it out and CHANGELOG.md in the project directory is used when it exists. A release heading is ## x.y.z , where x.y.z is the version in your config. A date may follow: ## x.y.z - 2026-09-19 . The notes are everything below that heading up to the next ## heading. Text above the first release heading, such as the title or an introduction, is never published. Use ### for groups such as "Added" and "Fixed" if you like; they stay inside the section. A section may hold at most 16 KiB. Put the newest release at the top. Write for the people who use the app: what changed for them, not the commit history. Publishing fails with CHANGELOG.md has no notes for this release. Add a `## 1.2.0` section when the heading is missing or its section is empty, so a release cannot go out with the wrong notes. A project with no changelog at all publishes without notes; the update is still offered with its version number. The build also writes the extracted section to dist/<target>/release-notes.md . Where it appears How it is shown Windows and Linux Your app receives the Markdown unchanged as event.notes . Render it with the Markdown component, or show it as text. macOS Sparkle's update window renders it as Markdown. GitHub release page ( target = "github" ) It becomes the release description.

110.content: Variable Meaning AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID Access key with permission to write objects in the bucket AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY or S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY Its secret AWS_SESSION_TOKEN or S3_SESSION_TOKEN Only for temporary credentials For R2, create an API token with Object Read & Write on the bucket and use its access key ID and secret. If a CDN caches your bucket, give appcast-*.xml , latest-linux-<arch>.txt , and install.sh a short cache lifetime, because they change with every release.

111.hierarchy: Auto Updater › Publishing › Linux install command
111.content: Linux builds also publish install.sh . It installs the tarball into ~/.local/<package>.app without root, adds the app to the applications menu, and that install keeps itself up to date. Give users one line: Add | sh -s -- --uninstall to the same URL to remove it. Set linux.tarball = false to skip the tarball and script.

112.content: The app says it is up to date. The published version must be higher than the installed one, the release must not be a draft or pre-release on GitHub, and the feed for that target must exist. Open the feed URL from the table above in a browser to check. Set updates.publicKey and QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY . The build has no private key. Export the variable or set ed25519SecretKey . Update signing key does not match updates.publicKey . The private key is not the pair of the configured public key. Use the original key; apps in the field only trust that one. CHANGELOG.md has no notes for this release . Add a ## x.y.z heading that equals version exactly, with at least one line under it. The status is disabled . Development builds never update, and neither do .deb , system-wide, or root-owned Linux installs. Test with a production build. GitHub upload failed . Check gh auth status , that the token can write to the repository ( contents: write in Actions), and that the repository name is right. S3 upload failed . Check the credentials, region , and endpoint . A 403 on download means the bucket does not allow public reads.

113.content: The updater is linked into the executable. quickgui build detects the feature and stages the install helper beside it ( quickgui-updater-helper , or Sparkle.framework on macOS) from @quickgui/extension-updater at the same version. Current prebuilt packages cover macOS; on other hosts run bun packages/native/build.ts --extension updater in a source checkout first.

114.content: Share Rust modules or author a native service for Go and TypeScript apps. A Rust app can share ordinary modules, or it can author a native extension that Go and TypeScript apps load. Rust apps enable crate features instead of listing extensions in config.

115.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Choose an extension type
115.content: What you are adding What you ship Components or application logic A Rust module or crate Optional QuickGUI capabilities Cargo features such as updater and terminal A native service for Go or TypeScript A cdylib , a manifest, and a typed wrapper A Rust app already links quickgui . It does not load a separate host library.

116.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Create an extension project
116.content: Use this when Go or TypeScript apps should consume a native service. --npm-package sets the artifact package name.

117.content: Export functions that return Element : Return notice("Saved") as a child. Keep application-wide services outside View::render .

118.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Lay out a native extension
118.content: A native extension ships quickgui.extension.json , a versioned shared library, and declared resources. Rust extensions can vendor extension_api.rs and build a cdylib without linking the renderer. See the Go Authoring Extensions guide for the native contract.

119.content: Rust applications enable features in Cargo.toml . Keep the crate version already in your project: Go and TypeScript consumers declare the extension package in their own config.

120.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Implement the native contract
120.content: Implement invoke and shutdown . Copy borrowed input before returning, keep events scoped to their sessions, and release workers when a session stops.

121.content: Go and TypeScript CLIs bundle declared extensions. A Rust app has nothing extra to register: Cargo links the crates you depend on.

122.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Build and package artifacts
122.content: App edits rebuild the selected crate. Rebuild an extension when its native implementation changes, then rebuild the consuming Go or TypeScript app.

148.content: SyntaxLanguage selects a registered Tree-sitter grammar and highlight query. Query captures are flattened into eight stable SyntaxTheme classes and applied as foreground-only HighlightStyle spans, so color never changes text metrics. Source or language changes reparse the bounded document; palette changes only remap the retained captures, and scrolling does no syntax work. Parsing is limited to 2 MiB, individual lines over 32 KiB stay plain, and the capture count is capped. This is structural syntax highlighting, not language-server semantic tokens.

183.content: Checkbox pub fn new(state: impl Into<ToggleState>) -> Self parent pub fn parent(children: impl IntoIterator<Item = bool>) -> Self Derive a parent checkbox from the checked values of the boxes it governs. This is Base UI's `parent` checkbox: every child checked reports on, none reports off, and a mix reports mixed. QuickGUI keeps no child registry — the application passes the values it is already rendering — so the derivation stays a pure function of the caller's own data. ``` use quickgui::{Checkbox, ToggleState}; assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, true]).state(), ToggleState::On); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([false, false]).state(), ToggleState::Off); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, false]).state(), ToggleState::Mixed); // An empty group is unchecked rather than mixed. assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([]).state(), ToggleState::Off); ``` read_only pub const fn read_only(mut self, read_only: bool) -> Self Show a value the user may read but not change, Base UI's `readOnly`. Unlike a disabled checkbox, a read-only one stays focusable and stays in the Tab sequence. Mixed and off both move to on, and on moves to off, which is the web's tri-state contract. A read-only checkbox returns `None`, so a click listener that asks before writing cannot change a value the control is refusing. parent_next_checked pub const fn parent_next_checked(self) -> Option<bool> The checked value activating a parent checkbox moves its whole group to. Add a menu-bar or notification-area icon, and mark macOS template images by filename or flag. A tray icon lives in the macOS menu bar, the Windows notification area, or a Linux StatusNotifierItem host. Put the artwork in resources/ and create the icon from the application startup callback. This is separate from the packaged App Icon .

Add a square PNG that is at least 256×256 pixels at resources/icon.png . 1024×1024 is a good source. quickgui build resizes it to every size macOS, Windows, and Linux need. The CLI writes .icns for macOS, .ico for the Windows installer, and the Freedesktop hicolor sizes for Linux. Development reloads skip generated containers; production builds and a configured macos.icon still install an icon. Optional resources/icon.iconset/icon_<n>x<n>.png files replace a generated size with a hand-drawn one. That folder is a build input and is not copied into the packaged app. Set icon in the CLI config only when the source PNG lives somewhere other than resources/icon.png .

Add the private key as a repository secret named QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), then push a tag that matches the version in your config: The three jobs upload into the same release. The gh CLI is preinstalled on GitHub's runners. macOS builds that you distribute should also pass --sign and --notarize ; Windows needs NSIS ( makensis ) on the runner, and Linux produces an AppImage only when appimagetool is installed (the tarball needs nothing).

This is Base UI's `parent` checkbox: every child checked reports on, none reports off, and a mix reports mixed. QuickGUI keeps no child registry — the application passes the values it is already rendering — so the derivation stays a pure function of the caller's own data. ``` use quickgui::{Checkbox, ToggleState}; assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, true]).state(), ToggleState::On); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([false, false]).state(), ToggleState::Off); assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([true, false]).state(), ToggleState::Mixed); // An empty group is unchecked rather than mixed. assert_eq!(Checkbox::parent([]).state(), ToggleState::Off); ``` read_only pub const fn read_only(mut self, read_only: bool) -> Self Show a value the user may read but not change, Base UI's `readOnly`. Unlike a disabled checkbox, a read-only one stays focusable and stays in the Tab sequence. Mixed and off both move to on, and on moves to off, which is the web's tri-state contract. A read-only checkbox returns `None`, so a click listener that asks before writing cannot change a value the control is refusing. parent_next_checked pub const fn parent_next_checked(self) -> Option<bool> The checked value activating a parent checkbox moves its whole group to. DiffView uses the same registered Tree-sitter grammars as Editor. When its document, language, or syntax palette changes, it parses each visible old/new file lane once and assigns capture fragments to logical rows. Each RenderSide then builds and caches its StyledText lazily when mounted, merging inline addition/deletion emphasis at non-overlapping byte boundaries. Scrolling never invokes the parser.

Every update is signed with an Ed25519 key. Create the pair once and keep it for the life of the app: installs only accept updates signed by the key they were built with. The command writes quickgui-update.pub and quickgui-update.key . The public key is safe to commit; the config below reads it from update-public-key.pub . The .key file is the secret: store it in a password manager or your CI secret store, never in the repository. If you lose it, existing installs can never update again.

On macOS, a template image is a monochrome mask. AppKit recolors it for the menu bar's light, dark, and highlighted appearances using only the alpha channel. A filename whose stem ends in Template , optionally followed by @2x or @3x , is treated as a template: trayTemplate.png and statusTemplate@2x.png match. emailTemplateIcon.png does not. quickgui::is_template_image_path is the same check. Call .template(true) or .icon_is_template(true) when the name does not follow that convention, or .template(false) to force the flag off. Image , MenuIcon , and TrayIconImage all carry the flag. Other platforms keep it and ignore it.

Raise version in your config first: apps only install a version higher than their own. Add a ## <version> section to CHANGELOG.md for it. Then give the build the private key and run it with --upload : For GitHub, sign in once with gh auth login (or set GH_TOKEN ). For S3, set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY . --upload builds the app, signs the update files, writes the feed, and publishes everything. It prints each public URL when it finishes. Use --update-manifest instead to sign and write the feed without uploading, for example to inspect dist/ first. Run the command once per target; every target has its own feed, so a Mac never downloads a Linux build.

Release notes come from one Markdown changelog that covers every version. When you publish version 1.2.0 , the build takes the section under the ## 1.2.0 heading and ships it with the update. updates.changelog names the file, relative to the project. Leave it out and CHANGELOG.md in the project directory is used when it exists. A release heading is ## x.y.z , where x.y.z is the version in your config. A date may follow: ## x.y.z - 2026-09-19 . The notes are everything below that heading up to the next ## heading. Text above the first release heading, such as the title or an introduction, is never published. Use ### for groups such as "Added" and "Fixed" if you like; they stay inside the section. A section may hold at most 16 KiB. Put the newest release at the top. Write for the people who use the app: what changed for them, not the commit history. Publishing fails with CHANGELOG.md has no notes for this release. Add a `## 1.2.0` section when the heading is missing or its section is empty, so a release cannot go out with the wrong notes. A project with no changelog at all publishes without notes; the update is still offered with its version number. The build also writes the extracted section to dist/<target>/release-notes.md . Where it appears How it is shown Windows and Linux Your app receives the Markdown unchanged as event.notes . Render it with the Markdown component, or show it as text. macOS Sparkle's update window renders it as Markdown. GitHub release page ( target = "github" ) It becomes the release description.

Set updates.target to "github" or "s3" , and fill in the section with the same name. The target decides where --upload sends files and which URLs the app checks, so you never write a feed or download URL yourself. Both sections may stay in the config; only the one target names is used. The feed address is built into the app, so changing target later only affects versions built after the change. Keep publishing to the old target until users have moved over. GitHub Releases needs only the repository. It must be public, because installed apps download updates without credentials. Amazon S3 needs the bucket, its region, and the public HTTPS address that serves it (the bucket's own URL, or a CloudFront domain in front of it). Cloudflare R2, MinIO, and other S3-compatible stores add endpoint , the address of the S3 API. publicUrl is still the address users download from, which for R2 is a custom domain or the bucket's r2.dev URL. The bucket has to allow public reads of the uploaded files; QuickGUI uploads with your credentials but does not change bucket policy. Enable the crate feature. Share Rust modules or author a native service for Go and TypeScript apps. A Rust app can share ordinary modules, or it can author a native extension that Go and TypeScript apps load. Rust apps enable crate features instead of listing extensions in config.

Ship a small PNG with the app, then create the icon from its packaged path: set_tray_icon replaces the icon with that id. remove_tray_icon deletes it. Image::open and TrayIconImage::from_path both honor the template filename convention. A 22×22 PNG is a good 1× source. Draw a 44×44 companion as trayTemplate@2x.png when you want a retina menu-bar image.

Ship files in resources/ and load them from the packaged resource directory. Put application files that are not compiled into the executable in a resources/ directory: images, templates, JSON, and other data. The CLI copies that directory’s contents into the packaged app. The running app reads them from AppPaths::resource_dir() , which does not depend on the launch working directory. To embed bytes at compile time instead, use BundledAssets and Application::assets . Custom fonts are a separate option. See Fonts .

Ship signed automatic updates for macOS, Windows, and Linux. Enable the updater feature on the quickgui crate. The updater is part of the Rust core, so Rust apps call quickgui::updater directly. Go and TypeScript load the same implementation as an extension, with the same feed, key, and install helper.

Start one Updater after the application is ready and read its events on the application thread: quickgui::updater_options!() expands to the settings quickgui build embedded. With plain cargo run it is empty, and the updater reports Disabled , as every development build does. Call updater.check().await from a Check for Updates action, updater.install().await from an update banner, and updater.set_automatic_checks(enabled).await from settings. Each resolves when the command is accepted or rejected; results arrive as events. updater.state() returns the latest event without native calls.

SyntaxLanguage selects a registered Tree-sitter grammar and highlight query. Query captures are flattened into eight stable SyntaxTheme classes and applied as foreground-only HighlightStyle spans, so color never changes text metrics. Source or language changes reparse the bounded document; palette changes only remap the retained captures, and scrolling does no syntax work. Parsing is limited to 2 MiB, individual lines over 32 KiB stay plain, and the capture count is capped. This is structural syntax highlighting, not language-server semantic tokens.

SyntaxLanguage selects a registered Tree-sitter grammar and its highlight query. Captures are flattened into eight stable SyntaxTheme classes and applied as foreground-only HighlightStyle spans, so color does not change text metrics. Parsing happens when source or language changes; scrolling only mounts rows and lazily creates their StyledText . Parsing is limited to 2 MiB, individual lines over 32 KiB stay plain, and the capture count is capped.

The app says it is up to date. The published version must be higher than the installed one, the release must not be a draft or pre-release on GitHub, and the feed for that target must exist. Open the feed URL from the table above in a browser to check. Set updates.publicKey and QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY . The build has no private key. Export the variable or set ed25519SecretKey . Update signing key does not match updates.publicKey . The private key is not the pair of the configured public key. Use the original key; apps in the field only trust that one. CHANGELOG.md has no notes for this release . Add a ## x.y.z heading that equals version exactly, with at least one line under it. The status is disabled . Development builds never update, and neither do .deb , system-wide, or root-owned Linux installs. Test with a production build. GitHub upload failed . Check gh auth status , that the token can write to the repository ( contents: write in Actions), and that the repository name is right. S3 upload failed . Check the credentials, region , and endpoint . A 403 on download means the bucket does not allow public reads.

The packaged icon is the application identity. A window can show a different image on Windows and X11: After the window exists, cx.set_window_icon(icon) and cx.clear_window_icon() update that image. On macOS, windows do not have their own icon. Use cx.set_dock_icon(icon) to replace the Dock image for this process. Menu-bar and notification-area icons are a different image. See Tray Icon .

The target fixes every address. <file> is a name such as appcast-darwin-arm64.xml , and <tag> is tagPrefix plus the version. GitHub S3 Update feed, install.sh , latest-linux-<arch>.txt https://github.com/<repository>/releases/latest/download/<file> <publicUrl>/<prefix>/<file> Installers and update archives https://github.com/<repository>/releases/download/<tag>/<file> <publicUrl>/<prefix>/<file> On GitHub the feed always comes from the release marked Latest . Drafts and pre-releases are never latest, so they do not reach users until you publish them as a normal release. The CLI embeds the version, identifier, feed URL, and public key in the app. Secret keys are never embedded.

The tray menu is a native context menu. Handle TrayEventKind::MenuItem on Application::on_tray_event . Other kinds are Click , DoubleClick , Enter , Move , Leave , and Scroll . show_tray_menu opens the menu at the cursor on macOS and Windows. Linux hosts own menu presentation and reject that call.

The updater is linked into the executable. quickgui build detects the feature and stages the install helper beside it ( quickgui-updater-helper , or Sparkle.framework on macOS) from @quickgui/extension-updater at the same version. Current prebuilt packages cover macOS; on other hosts run bun packages/native/build.ts --extension updater in a source checkout first.

Use resources/icon.png as the packaged application icon, or change the window or Dock icon at runtime. The packaged application icon is the image Finder, the Dock, the Windows taskbar, Start Menu, and Linux desktop launchers show for your app. Put a PNG at resources/icon.png . You can also change a window icon or the macOS Dock icon while the app is running.

Use the resources config option to merge extra files or folders into the same packaged directory. Each extra path is copied under its basename. Do not list the project resources/ folder here; it is included automatically. legal/NOTICE.txt is installed as NOTICE.txt . vendor/data is installed as data/ .

Use these when you already have a platform container: resources/icon.icns is used on macOS when macos.icon is omitted. resources/icon.ico is used by the NSIS installer when windows.icon is omitted. linux.icon is a square PNG used when both resources/icon.png and icon are omitted. macos.icon must be an .icns . windows.icon is an .ico . These config paths override the files in resources/ . Document-type icons are a basename inside the packaged resources. See Bundled Resources .
